name: AWS - S3 Bucket Download & Git History Credential Mining
command:
aws --profile <profile> s3 sync s3://<bucket_name> ./<local_dir>/
cd <local_dir>
git log
git show <commit_hash>
gitleaks detect --source . --verbose
description: Attackers with S3 read access can download entire buckets with 's3 sync'. Repositories stored in S3 may contain a .git directory — mining git commit history often reveals secrets (API keys, passwords) that were committed then 'deleted' but remain in history. gitleaks automates regex-based secret detection across the full working tree and all commits. Manual git show on suspicious commits reveals exact credential values and context.
source: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 25: Attacking AWS Cloud Infrastructure (25.4.1, 25.4.2)

examples.label: List S3 buckets to find interesting ones
Download a single file from S3
Sync entire S3 bucket to local directory
Check if downloaded content is a git repository
View full git commit history
examples.command:
cd offseclab-app-source && git log
# Commits with messages like 'removed key' or 'fix credentials' are high-value targets

examples.label: Show diff of a specific commit (find deleted secrets)
examples.command:
git show a1b2c3d4e5f6
# Lines starting with '-' were removed — these often contain the actual credentials

examples.label: Decode base64-encoded credential found in git history
Automated secret scan with gitleaks (all commits + working tree)
examples.command:
gitleaks detect --source . --verbose
# Returns: leakID, ruleID, secret value, file, commit, author, date

examples.label: Configure found credentials as a new AWS profile
examples.command:
aws configure --profile found-creds
# Enter: Access Key ID, Secret Access Key, region
aws --profile found-creds sts get-caller-identity

notes: S3-hosted git repositories are a common finding when developers push source code to S3 for CI/CD or artifact storage. The .git directory stores the entire history — deleting a file in a new commit does NOT remove it from prior commits. 'git log --all --full-history' shows all commits including in detached branches. 'git grep <pattern> $(git rev-list --all)' searches all commits for a specific pattern without checking out each commit. gitleaks uses entropy-based and regex rules to detect API keys, passwords, private keys, connection strings across many common services (AWS, GitHub, Stripe, etc.). Always decode any base64 strings found — AWS access key IDs start with 'AKIA' (long-term) or 'ASIA' (temporary/STS).

references.title: OffSec PEN-200 - Attacking AWS Cloud Infrastructure
MITRE ATT&CK - Credentials from Cloud Storage

recommended.note: Enumerate accessible S3 buckets before downloading content.
Configure AWS profile with compromised credentials before syncing.
Use discovered AWS keys to enumerate what permissions the found identity has.

defense.why_it_works: S3 buckets misconfigured as public often contain sensitive files: .git directories (exposing full source code and commit history including hardcoded credentials), configuration files (.env, config.yaml with API keys/DB passwords), backup files, and CI/CD artifacts. Developers frequently commit AWS credentials to git repositories and then expose those repositories via misconfigured S3. Git history preserves credentials even after they're 'deleted' from current code.
defense.prerequisites: S3 bucket publicly accessible (no authentication). aws s3 ls or HTTP GET to enumerate bucket contents. git-dumper tool for extracting .git directories. truffleHog, git-secrets, or grep for credential extraction.
defense.impact: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata + T1213.003 Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories. Extracts credentials from exposed S3 buckets containing git repositories or config files — typically AWS keys, database credentials, API tokens. One S3 bucket with .env can compromise the entire application stack.
defense.detection:
S3 server access logs: GetObject calls from unexpected IPs for sensitive file paths (.env, .git/). CloudTrail: S3 GetObject events. GuardDuty: 'Discovery:S3/MaliciousIPCaller' or 'Exfiltration:S3/ObjectRead.Unusual'. CloudWatch: access to known sensitive file patterns.
Unusual access to bash history, registry credential paths, or private key files by unauthorized or scripting tools (DET0412/AN1153).
Reading of sensitive files like .bash_history, /etc/shadow, or private key directories by unauthorized users (AN1154).
Unusual access to ~/Library/Keychains, ~/.bash_history, or Terminal command history by unauthorized processes (AN1155).
Unauthorized API or console calls to retrieve or reset password credentials, download key material, or modify SSO settings (AN1157).
Configuration backup utilities or CLI access dumping plaintext passwords, local user hashes, or SNMP strings (AN1159).
defense.artifacts: S3 access log: GetObject for .git/config, .env, credentials.yaml | CloudTrail: ListObjects + GetObject burst | GuardDuty: S3 exfiltration finding | CloudWatch: alarm on .env file access
defense.prevention:
S3 Block Public Access: enable at the account level — prevents all public S3 access as a safety net. Secret scanning in CI/CD (git-secrets, truffleHog, GitHub Advanced Security) — catches credentials before they reach git history. S3 bucket policies: default-deny, require authentication. Pre-commit hooks: block commits with credential patterns. AWS Secrets Manager instead of .env files.
Active Directory Configuration: Remove vulnerable Group Policy Preferences (patch KB2962486).
Audit: Proactively search for files containing credentials; take remediation action when found.
Encrypt Sensitive Information: Store keys on separate cryptographic hardware rather than local system.
Filter Network Traffic: Limit access to Instance Metadata API; use WAF to prevent SSRF exploitation.
Operating System Configuration: Disable/restrict NTLM; consider set +o history and ln -s /dev/null ~/.bash_history.
Password Policies: Use strong passphrases for private keys; prohibit password storage in files or Registry.
Privileged Account Management: Limit permissions on Registry-stored credentials to minimize abuse.
Restrict File and Directory Permissions: Restrict file shares to specific directories with need-to-know access.
Update Software: Apply KB2962486 to prevent credentials being stored in GPPs.
defense.evasion: Use single HTTP request rather than aws s3 ls (avoids AWS credentials). Target known sensitive paths directly. Exfiltrate slowly to avoid GuardDuty rate-based detections.
defense.misconfiguration: S3 Block Public Access not enabled at account level. Bucket ACL or policy grants public read. Developer committed .env or AWS credentials to git repo. No secret scanning in CI/CD pipeline. S3 access logging not enabled.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Public bucket check:
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket vulnerable-bucket
# → Grants: [{Grantee: {Type: Group, URI: AllUsers}, Permission: READ}]
# → World-readable bucket

# Block Public Access disabled:
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket vulnerable-bucket
# → All 4 flags: false = no protection

# Developer committed credentials:
# .env file in bucket: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
defense.secure_config:
# Enable S3 Block Public Access at account level (prevents all public S3):
aws s3control put-public-access-block --account-id ACCOUNT_ID --public-access-block-configuration \
  'BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true'
